statement: Dad cuts a long stick into 5 pieces. Each cut goes straight across just one piece. How many cuts does he make?

choices.misconception: I drew the stick but missed the cut between the last two pieces.
I thought each piece needs its own cut, so 5 pieces need 5 cuts.
I counted the two ends of the stick as cuts as well as the cuts in between.
I thought every piece needs two cuts, one at each end.

hints: Draw the stick and mark the cuts.
Draw a line for the stick and split it into 5 pieces. The cuts are the marks between pieces. The two ends of the stick are not cuts.
Between 5 pieces in a row there is one gap after each piece except the last.

solutions.reliable: Draw the stick split into 5 pieces. The cuts sit between neighbouring pieces: between pieces 1 and 2, 2 and 3, 3 and 4, and 4 and 5. That is 4 cuts. The idea to keep: in a row, the gaps between things are one fewer than the things.

whyOnTest: The gap-versus-piece question is the gentlest form of the off-by-one trap, and a quick drawing settles it.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
